rows.question: When does my maternity leave start if my due date is 15 November 2026?
rows.reply:
Under the Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) rules, the protection period before birth covers the last six weeks before delivery. MuSchG §3(1) says your employer may not employ you "in den letzten sechs Wochen vor der Entbindung" (in the last six weeks before the birth).

The start is counted from the expected due date shown on your doctor's or midwife's certificate ("der voraussichtliche Tag der Entbindung … wie er sich aus dem ärztlichen Zeugnis oder dem Zeugnis einer Hebamme … ergibt"). If that certificate gives 15 November 2026, six weeks earlier is 4 October 2026. The excerpts do not set out how the individual days are counted.

Other points from the law:

- You may keep working during these six weeks only if you expressly say you are willing to. You can withdraw that statement at any time, with effect for the future.
- If the baby is not born on the expected day, the period before birth becomes shorter or longer to match.
- After the birth, your employer may not employ you for eight weeks. This rises to twelve weeks for a premature birth, for a multiple birth, or if a disability in the child is medically confirmed within eight weeks of the birth. For a confirmed disability, the extension applies only if you apply for it.
- If the baby comes early, the period after birth is extended by the time lost from the period before birth.

The law asks you to tell your employer you are pregnant and give the expected due date as soon as you know (MuSchG §15).

These rules are in the Mutterschutzgesetz, which applies to employees. The official family portal notes that self-employed women are not covered by it.

rows.question: How long after birth can we apply for Elterngeld without losing money?
rows.reply:
The law does not set a deadline for applying for Elterngeld (parental allowance). What it limits is how far back payment goes.

BEEG §7(1) says Elterngeld is paid retroactively only for the last three months of the child's life before the start of the month of life in which the application is received: "Es wird rückwirkend nur für die letzten drei Lebensmonate vor Beginn des Lebensmonats geleistet, in dem der Antrag auf Elterngeld eingegangen ist." The months counted are the child's months of life, not calendar months. Elterngeld can be received from the day of birth (BEEG §4(1)).

So an application received during the child's fourth month of life can still be paid back to the first month. Applications received later lose whole months of payment: any month of life before those three is not paid. The application must be made in writing ("Elterngeld ist schriftlich zu beantragen").

Whether you qualify and how much you receive is decided by your Elterngeldstelle, the office that issues the Elterngeld decision.

rows.question: How much notice do I have to give my employer for Elternzeit?
rows.reply:
Elternzeit (parental leave (unpaid job-protected leave)) is not applied for with an office. You request it from your employer in text form. BEEG §16(1) sets two notice periods, depending on when the leave falls:

- For leave before your child's third birthday: at least seven weeks before the leave begins ("spätestens sieben Wochen").
- For leave between the third birthday and the end of the child's eighth year: at least 13 weeks before the leave begins ("spätestens 13 Wochen").

The statute requires the request "in Textform" (text form). The official family portal explains that this can be a letter without a signature or an email.

When you request leave for the period before the third birthday, you must also state at the same time which periods within two years you will take as Elternzeit.

If there are urgent reasons, a reasonable shorter notice period is possible as an exception ("Bei dringenden Gründen ist ausnahmsweise eine angemessene kürzere Frist möglich"). The family portal names premature births and an adoption placement that could not be planned in time as examples. It says the period that then applies depends on the individual case.

For mothers: if a mother takes Elternzeit directly after the maternity protection period, that period counts toward the two-year period mentioned above. If she cannot request leave in time for a reason she is not responsible for, BEEG §16(2) lets her make the request within one week after that reason ends.

Your employer must confirm your Elternzeit to you ("Der Arbeitgeber hat ... die Elternzeit zu bescheinigen").

The family portal says that a single seven-week period applies for children born before 1 July 2015. The statutory excerpts here do not contain that transitional rule. If your child was born before that date, check the rule that applies to you with the official family portal.

rows.question: How long is maternity protection after the birth if the baby comes early?
rows.reply:
Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) after the birth normally lasts eight weeks. The law says the employer may not employ a woman "bis zum Ablauf von acht Wochen nach der Entbindung" (until eight weeks after the delivery have passed). The answer for an early baby depends on which of two situations applies.

If the baby simply arrives before the expected date, the period before the birth is shortened. The law adds that shortfall to the period after the birth: "Bei vorzeitiger Entbindung verlängert sich die Schutzfrist nach der Entbindung … um den Zeitraum der Verkürzung der Schutzfrist vor der Entbindung." So the eight weeks after the birth are extended by the days the baby came early.

If the birth counts as a premature birth ("Frühgeburten" in the statute), the period after the birth is extended to twelve weeks. The same early-delivery rule then adds the days lost before the birth on top of those twelve weeks. The official family portal gives one example of a premature birth in the medical sense: a baby weighing less than 2,500 grams at birth. The statute itself does not define the term.

The law lists three grounds for the twelve-week period:
1. premature births;
2. multiple births;
3. a disability in the child, diagnosed by a doctor before eight weeks after the birth have passed. This third ground applies only if the woman applies for it ("nur, wenn die Frau dies beantragt").

The twelve-week extension does not apply to a stillbirth.

After the birth, the protection period cannot be waived by employees. Pupils and students are the exception. If an employer still demands work during this period, the family portal says you can contact your supervisory authority.

rows.question: Can my employer dismiss me while I am pregnant?
rows.reply:
In general, no. During pregnancy your employer may dismiss you only in rare exceptional cases, and only with official approval.

What the law protects. Under MuSchG §17(1), dismissal of a woman is not permitted ("Die Kündigung gegenüber einer Frau ist unzulässig"):
1. during her pregnancy,
2. until four months after a miscarriage after the twelfth week of pregnancy, and
3. until the end of her protection period after the birth, and at least until four months after the birth.

This Kündigungsschutz (protection against dismissal) applies if the employer knows of the pregnancy, miscarriage or birth when dismissing you, or is told within two weeks after you receive the dismissal ("innerhalb von zwei Wochen nach Zugang der Kündigung"). Missing those two weeks does no harm if the delay was not your fault and you inform the employer without delay. The same rules apply to steps an employer takes to prepare a dismissal. According to the official family portal, the protection also applies if you did not yet know you were pregnant, but you must already have been pregnant when you received the dismissal.

The exception. Under MuSchG §17(2), the highest state authority responsible for occupational safety, or a body it designates, can exceptionally declare a dismissal permissible in special cases that are not connected with your condition during pregnancy, after a miscarriage or after the birth. Such a dismissal must be in writing and must state the reason. The family portal gives examples of such cases: the company is insolvent, the business is partly closed down, a small business cannot continue without a qualified replacement, or a particularly serious breach of duty. The portal says that without the authority's approval the dismissal is invalid ("unwirksam").

If you are dismissed anyway. The family portal says that if you are dismissed without the authority's approval, you must bring a claim before the labour court. It says the claim must "normalerweise innerhalb von 3 Wochen" (normally within 3 weeks) be filed after you receive the written dismissal. If you do not file a claim, the dismissal is treated as effective. The portal also says you should involve the responsible supervisory authority. If the authority did approve the dismissal, you can challenge that approval separately. That challenge does not replace the claim at the labour court.

The family portal also says this protection can be extended if you take Elternzeit after the birth.

Whether a particular dismissal is permissible is decided by the state authority responsible for occupational safety and, in a dispute, by the labour court. In Hessen, that means the authority responsible for occupational safety in the state.

rows.question: Is there an income limit above which we get no Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes. Under BEEG §1(8), the entitlement to Elterngeld (parental allowance) lapses ("Ein Anspruch entfällt") if the entitled person had zu versteuerndes Einkommen (taxable income) of "mehr als 175 000 Euro" in the last completed tax assessment period before the child's birth.

Where another person also meets the conditions, for example by also living in a household with the child, the incomes are added together. The entitlement lapses if "die Summe des zu versteuernden Einkommens beider Personen mehr als 175 000 Euro beträgt" (the combined taxable income of both is more than 175,000 euros).

The limit refers to zu versteuerndes Einkommen, not gross pay. The Familienportal explains that gross income is usually much higher than taxable income. It also says the Finanzamt determines taxable income and states it in the Steuerbescheid (tax assessment).

If the tax assessment for the last completed period before the birth is not yet available when you apply:
- BEEG §8(2): if the application indicates the limit will probably not be exceeded, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation in case the limit turns out to be exceeded.
- BEEG §8(3): if it cannot yet be said whether the limit is exceeded, the amount is decided provisionally until the required information is provided.

The Familienportal states that different limits applied to births before 1 April 2025. The excerpts here do not include the statute's transitional provision for earlier births, so I cannot say which limit applies to a particular birth date.

Whether the limit affects your family is decided by the Elterngeldstelle for your district, not by this service.

rows.question: How many months of Elterngeld can we get in total?
rows.reply:
Elterngeld (parental allowance) is paid in monthly amounts for the child's months of life, not calendar months. BEEG §4 sets these limits.

Joint entitlement: the parents together are entitled to twelve monthly amounts of basic Elterngeld ("zwölf Monatsbeträge Basiselterngeld"). If one parent's earned income is reduced in two months of the child's life, the parents together get two further months ("zwei weitere Monate Basiselterngeld (Partnermonate)"). That makes 14 months in total.

Per parent: one parent can receive at most twelve monthly amounts of basic Elterngeld. On top of that, they can receive at most four monthly amounts of the partnership bonus under § 4b ("zuzüglich der höchstens vier zustehenden Monatsbeträge Partnerschaftsbonus nach § 4b"). A parent only has a claim if they receive Elterngeld for at least two months of the child's life. Months in which a parent receives certain benefits credited under § 3 count as months of basic Elterngeld for that parent.

The Plus variant: instead of one month of basic Elterngeld, a parent can take two months of Elterngeld Plus ("jeweils zwei Lebensmonate Elterngeld Plus").

Time window: basic Elterngeld can be received until the child completes the 14th month of life. Elterngeld Plus can be received until the child completes the 32nd month of life. This only applies as long as, from the 15th month, at least one parent takes it in consecutive months.

Premature births: the joint entitlement to basic Elterngeld is higher for a child born:
- at least 6 weeks before the expected due date: 13 monthly amounts;
- at least 8 weeks before: 14;
- at least 12 weeks before: 15;
- at least 16 weeks before: 16.
In these cases, the per-parent maximum rises to 13, 14, 15 or 16 monthly amounts plus up to four partnership bonus months. The window for basic Elterngeld extends to the 15th, 16th, 17th or 18th month of life. The expected due date is the one shown in the doctor's or midwife's certificate.

The conditions for the partnership bonus are set out in § 4b, which is not among the excerpts here. The federal Familienportal describes it as up to 4 additional months for each parent if both work part-time in parallel.

How many months your family receives is decided by the Elterngeld office for your district.

rows.question: What is the Partnerschaftsbonus and who qualifies?
rows.reply:
The Partnerschaftsbonus (partnership bonus months) gives each parent extra months of parental allowance paid at the ElterngeldPlus rate. Under BEEG §4b(1), each parent receives "einen zusätzlichen Monatsbetrag Elterngeld Plus" (an additional monthly amount of ElterngeldPlus) for a month of the child's life when both of these conditions are met:

1. Both parents work at least 24 and at most 32 hours a week, averaged over that month of the child's life ("nicht weniger als 24 und nicht mehr als 32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats").
2. Both parents meet the general conditions of BEEG §1. The excerpts do not set out what §1 contains.

Further rules in BEEG §4b:

- Each parent can receive at most four bonus months. It can only be taken for at least two months (§4b(2)).
- Both parents must take it at the same time, in consecutive months of the child's life (§4b(3)).
- Suppose it later turns out that the conditions were not met in every month applied for. The consecutive-months requirement still counts as met (§4b(5)).
- If one of the conditions for sole receipt in §4c(1) nos. 1 to 3 arises while the bonus is being paid, one parent can continue receiving it under §4c(2) (§4b(4)).

One parent alone can also receive these extra months (BEEG §4c(2)). That parent must work 24 to 32 hours a week on average, in two to four consecutive months. One of these three grounds in §4c(1) must also apply:

1. The parent meets the conditions for the tax relief for single parents under §24b(1) and (3) of the Income Tax Act. The other parent also lives neither with them nor with the child.
2. Care by the other parent would endanger the child's welfare within the meaning of §1666(1) and (2) of the Civil Code.
3. Care by the other parent is impossible, in particular because of serious illness or severe disability. Economic reasons and being busy with other activities are not taken into account.

Amount: the official family portal says the bonus is calculated the same way as ElterngeldPlus. Depending on income before the birth, it is between 150 and 900 euros per parent per month.

The same portal also notes something about which rules apply. Its explanations cover children born after August 2021. For children born before 1 September 2021, partly different rules apply, and it refers those parents to their Elterngeldstelle.

Whether you qualify, and how much you would receive, is decided only by the Elterngeldstelle responsible for you.

rows.question: How quickly do we have to register the birth at the Standesamt?
rows.reply:
The law sets a one-week period. Under PStG §18(1), the birth of a child must be reported to the Standesamt (civil registry office) for the district where the child was born "binnen einer Woche" (within one week).

The same section allows two ways of reporting:
- by the persons named in PStG §19, orally or in writing, or
- by the facilities named in PStG §20, in writing.

When the persons named in §19 make the report, they must substantiate the birth ("glaubhaft zu machen").

For a stillborn child, a shorter rule applies. The report must be made "spätestens am dritten auf die Geburt folgenden Werktag" (at the latest on the third working day after the birth).

The federal family portal explains what usually happens in practice:
- If the child is born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic, that facility notifies the responsible Standesamt and sends it the birth certificate.
- If the child is born at home, the midwife or doctor issues the birth certificate. You must then present it to the responsible Standesamt within one week.

The Standesamt for the place of birth is the responsible authority. Its website lists the further documents it asks for.

rows.question: What do we need to bring to the Standesamt to register the birth?
rows.reply:
Under the federal birth-registration regulation (PStV §33), when a birth is notified the Standesamt (civil registry office) should ask you to present the following:

1. If the parents are married to each other: your marriage certificate or a certified extract from the marriage register, plus your own birth certificates if your birth registration details are not shown on the marriage certificate. 2. If the parents are not married to each other: the mother's birth certificate. If paternity has already been acknowledged, also the acknowledgement declarations and the father's birth certificate, and any joint custody declarations.
3. Both parents' identity documents: an identity card, passport or other recognised passport-substitute document.
4. If the birth is notified orally: a certificate of the birth issued by a doctor or midwife who was present at the birth.

The Familienportal guidance adds that you need the birth certificate from the birth attendant. If your child was born at home, the midwife or doctor issues it and you must present it to the responsible Standesamt within one week. The responsible office is the Standesamt for the place where the child was born.

If the parents are not German citizens, the Standesamt will also ask at registration whether either parent has an unlimited right of residence (PStV §34). This is so it can check whether the child acquired German citizenship at birth. That decision is made by the Standesamt, using information it obtains from the Ausländerbehörde.

rows.question: Does my Krankenkasse pay for a midwife?
rows.reply:
Yes, as a rule. Under federal law, a woman insured with a Krankenkasse (statutory health insurer) is entitled to help from a Hebamme (midwife) during pregnancy, at the birth and after the birth. This includes the examinations to confirm the pregnancy and prenatal check-ups ("Anspruch auf ärztliche Betreuung sowie auf Hebammenhilfe einschließlich der Untersuchungen zur Feststellung der Schwangerschaft und zur Schwangerenvorsorge").

Midwife care after the birth has a time limit. It runs until twelve weeks after the birth. Anything beyond that needs a doctor's order ("bis zum Ablauf von zwölf Wochen nach der Geburt, weitergehende Leistungen bedürfen der ärztlichen Anordnung").

If the mother cannot care for the child after the birth, the insured child has its own entitlement to the midwife services that relate to the child.

The official family portal says the same in plain terms: every woman with statutory health insurance is entitled to support from a Hebamme. If you are privately insured, the portal says to check with your insurer beforehand which services it covers. Private insurance is outside what this product covers.

Whether a particular service is covered in your case is decided by your Krankenkasse. Contact your Krankenkasse directly.

rows.question: How do we insure the baby after the birth?
rows.reply:
Under federal law, a baby can be covered through Familienversicherung (free family cover for dependants) in the statutory health insurance of a parent who is a member of a statutory health insurance fund (SGB V §10).

What the law says:

- Children of members are insured if they meet all of these conditions (§10(1)): they live or ordinarily stay in Germany ("Wohnsitz oder gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt im Inland"); they are not compulsorily insured under the listed grounds of §5(1) and not voluntarily insured; they are not exempt from, or released from, compulsory insurance; they are not mainly self-employed; and their total income does not regularly exceed one seventh of the monthly reference value under §18 of the Fourth Book.
- Children are covered up to their 18th birthday, and in some cases longer (§10(2)).
- There is an exclusion (§10(3)). A child is not covered if the parent who is related to the child, and is the member's spouse or civil partner, is not a member of a statutory fund, and that parent's total income regularly exceeds one twelfth of the annual earnings ceiling ("Jahresarbeitsentgeltgrenze") and is regularly higher than the member's income.
- If the conditions are met through more than one parent, the member chooses the fund (§10(5)).
- The member must report the family-insured child to the responsible fund, with the details needed to run the Familienversicherung, and must report later changes (§10(6)).

The birth certificate: the registry office that issues it is the one responsible for the place of birth. You must register the child there within 1 week of the birth. The birth certificate is needed for the "Anmeldung bei der Krankenkasse" (registering with the health insurance fund).

These excerpts do not say what to do if the baby is not covered by Familienversicherung. They also do not give a time limit for reporting the baby to the fund.

Whether your baby is covered is decided by the parent's statutory health insurance fund, not here. Contact that fund to report the child.

rows.question: When are the first check-ups for the baby?
rows.reply:
The Kinder-Richtlinie, the federal directive on early detection of illness in children, sets out ten check-ups in the first six years of life ("insgesamt zehn Untersuchungen"). Each has a set period and a wider tolerance window. The directive says the check-ups "können nur in den jeweils angegebenen Zeiträumen unter Berücksichtigung folgender Toleranzgrenzen in Anspruch genommen werden": they can only be used within those periods, taking the tolerance limits into account.

The first four are:

- U1: immediately after birth ("Unmittelbar nach der Geburt"). It should be done within the first 30 minutes after the child is born ("innerhalb der ersten 30 Minuten nach der Geburt"). If no doctor is present at the birth but a midwife is, the midwife should carry it out.
- U2: 3rd to 10th day of life. Tolerance: 3rd to 14th day.
- U3: 4th to 5th week of life. Tolerance: 3rd to 8th week.
- U4: 3rd to 4th month of life. Tolerance: 2nd to 4½ month.

For babies born early, the same periods still apply ("Auch bei Frühgeborenen sind die Untersuchungszeiträume einzuhalten"). Being born early is taken into account when the results are assessed.

Under the same directive, children have a right to these early-detection check-ups until their 18th birthday.

rows.question: What is Mutterschaftsgeld and when do I apply for it?
rows.reply:
Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is a payment for the protection periods before and after the birth and for the day of birth itself (MuSchG §19, SGB V §24i(3)). The official family portal says these protection periods normally begin 6 weeks before the calculated due date and end 8 weeks after the birth.

The law sets out two routes.

Women insured with a statutory health insurer (gesetzliche Krankenkasse): Mutterschaftsgeld is paid under the Fifth Book of the Social Code (MuSchG §19(1)). SGB V §24i(1) names who receives it:
- members who are entitled to sickness benefit when unable to work;
- members who are not paid wages because of the protection periods under §3 MuSchG;
- women whose employment ends immediately before the protection period begins, if they were members of a health insurer on the last day of that employment.

For members who are employed when the protection period before the birth begins, it is calculated from average net daily pay over the last three settled calendar months before that period. It is "höchstens 13 Euro für den Kalendertag" (at most 13 euros per calendar day) (SGB V §24i(2)). Where average pay is higher, the employer pays the difference as a top-up to Mutterschaftsgeld (MuSchG §20(1)).

Women not in a statutory health insurer: Mutterschaftsgeld is paid by the federal government, "insgesamt höchstens 210 Euro" (at most 210 euros in total). It is paid "auf Antrag vom Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung" (on application, by the Federal Office for Social Security) (MuSchG §19(2)).

When to apply: the excerpts do not state when to apply or set any application deadline. They do say one thing that affects timing. For payment before the birth, the deciding document is a certificate from a doctor or midwife stating the expected day of delivery (SGB V §24i(3)).

For the timing and steps of your application, ask your Krankenkasse if you are statutorily insured. If you are not, ask the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung. That body or your Krankenkasse decides whether you are entitled and how much you receive.

rows.question: We are not married. Is my partner automatically the legal father?
rows.reply:
No. Under federal law, being the partner of the mother is not enough on its own. BGB §1592 says a child's father is the man who: 1. was married to the mother at the time of the birth ("zum Zeitpunkt der Geburt mit der Mutter des Kindes verheiratet"), 2. has acknowledged paternity ("die Vaterschaft anerkannt hat"), or 3. has had his paternity established by a court ("gerichtlich festgestellt").

For parents who are not married at the birth, the official family portal states that the father must make a Vaterschaftsanerkennung (acknowledgement of paternity) to count legally as the father. The acknowledgement is voluntary and needs the mother's consent.

What the law says about the acknowledgement:
- It can be made before the child is born (BGB §1594(4)).
- It is not effective while another man's paternity exists (BGB §1594(2)).
- It is invalid if made subject to a condition or a time limit (BGB §1594(3)).

Where it is made: the father must declare it in person at a competent office, for example the youth welfare office, a registry office, a local court or a notary. The mother must also declare her consent in person. The office records both. Depending on the federal state, it can cost a fee at a notary or a local court.

Parental custody is a separate step. If the parents are not married at the birth, the mother has parental custody from the birth. Acknowledging paternity does not by itself give the father custody. That also needs declarations by both parents that they want joint custody, or a court decision. Parents who marry after the birth also gain joint custody.

The portal names your local youth welfare office as the place that advises on custody questions.

rows.question: How do unmarried parents get joint custody?
rows.reply:
Under German law, if the parents are not married to each other when the child is born, the mother has parental custody from birth. The law gives three ways for the parents to hold custody jointly (BGB §1626a(1)):

1. Both parents declare that they want to take on custody jointly. This is the Sorgeerklärung (declaration of joint custody); each parent makes one.
2. The parents marry each other.
3. The family court transfers custody to them jointly.

Where none of these applies, the mother has custody ("Im Übrigen hat die Mutter die elterliche Sorge", BGB §1626a(3)).

The other parent must first be legally recognised as the father. According to the federal family portal, this happens either when he acknowledges the child as his own with the mother's consent, or when a court establishes paternity. Recognition of paternity does not by itself give custody. A Sorgeerklärung from both parents, or a court decision, is still needed.

The court route: on the application of one parent, the family court transfers custody, or part of it, to both parents jointly if this does not conflict with the child's welfare ("wenn die Übertragung dem Kindeswohl nicht widerspricht"). If the other parent puts forward no reasons against joint custody and none are otherwise apparent, the law presumes that joint custody does not conflict with the child's welfare (BGB §1626a(2)). The federal family portal adds that in this situation the court decides in a simplified procedure, without hearing the youth welfare office and without hearing the parents in person.

When a Sorgeerklärung is made, or a final court decision transfers custody jointly, an entry is made in the custody register kept by the responsible youth welfare office (SGB VIII §58(1)).

Parents who are not married to each other have a right to advice about making a Sorgeerklärung and about the possibility of a court transfer of joint custody (SGB VIII §18(2)). Your local youth welfare office (Jugendamt) is the office to approach for this advice. The excerpts do not describe where or in what form the declaration itself is made; the youth welfare office can tell you that.

rows.question: Where do we apply for Elterngeld in Frankfurt?
rows.reply:
You apply to the Elterngeld office responsible for the place where your child lives. By law, the Länder decide which authority handles Elterngeld (parental allowance). For a child living in Frankfurt, that means the Elterngeldstelle (the state office that decides parental allowance) responsible for Frankfurt.

You can submit the application at an Elterngeldstelle in person or digitally. Every Bundesland offers a digital application.

For Hessen, the Elterngeld page of the regional authority in Gießen lists current contact details for the six Hessian state offices and for the supervisory body for Elterngeld. It also links to a press release on applying online and on paper. The excerpts do not say which of the six offices covers Frankfurt; that page is where to check.

The application must be made in writing ("schriftlich zu beantragen"). Elterngeld is paid retroactively only for the last three months of the child's life before the month in which the application is received. Earlier months are not paid.

rows.question: Will our baby automatically be German if we are both Indian citizens?
rows.reply:
Not automatically because of your nationality alone. The law sets conditions, and whether your child meets them is decided by the authorities when the birth is registered.

The general rule: a child acquires deutsche Staatsangehörigkeit (citizenship) by birth if a parent is German (StAG §4(1)).

For a child of foreign parents, StAG §4(3) says the child acquires German citizenship by birth in Germany ("Durch die Geburt im Inland erwirbt ein Kind ausländischer Eltern die deutsche Staatsangehörigkeit") if one parent meets both of these conditions:
1. has lawfully had their habitual residence in Germany for five years ("seit fünf Jahren rechtmäßig seinen gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt im Inland"), and
2. holds an unlimited right of residence ("ein unbefristetes Aufenthaltsrecht"), or, as a Swiss citizen or a family member of one, a residence permit under the 1999 EU–Switzerland agreement on free movement.

Only one parent needs to meet both conditions. Where the child acquires citizenship this way, it is entered in the birth register ("Geburtenregister") where the birth is recorded.

How it is checked (PStV §34): when the birth is reported, the registry office ("das Standesamt") asks whether a parent has an unlimited right of residence. If the information indicates so, the Standesamt obtains written information from the immigration authority ("Ausländerbehörde") on whether this is correct and whether the parent had five years of lawful habitual residence in Germany at the time of the birth. The Standesamt then examines whether the child acquired German citizenship and records the result.

Whether your child meets these conditions is decided by the Standesamt that registers the birth, not here. The Standesamt where the birth is registered is the office to approach.

rows.question: Does our newborn need a residence permit?
rows.reply:
The law sets out several situations for a child born in Germany to foreign parents. Which one applies to your child is not something this answer can decide.

1. Aufenthaltserlaubnis (residence permit) for a child born in Germany (AufenthG §33):
- If one parent holds an Aufenthaltserlaubnis, a settlement permit or an EU long-term residence permit, the child "kann ... von Amts wegen eine Aufenthaltserlaubnis erteilt werden". It may be granted without an application, but this is not automatic.
- If at the time of birth both parents, or the parent who alone has custody, hold one of those permits, the child is granted the Aufenthaltserlaubnis without an application ("wird ... von Amts wegen erteilt").
- If the mother or father holds a visa at the time of birth, or may stay without a visa, the child's stay "gilt bis zum Ablauf des Visums oder des rechtmäßigen visumfreien Aufenthalts als erlaubt". The child's stay counts as permitted until that visa or visa-free stay ends.

2. German citizenship by birth (StAG §4). A child does not hold a foreign status in every case:
- A child acquires German citizenship at birth if one parent is a German citizen (§4(1)).
- A child of foreign parents born in Germany acquires German citizenship if one parent meets both of these conditions (§4(3)):
  - has lawfully had their habitual residence in Germany for five years ("seit fünf Jahren rechtmäßig seinen gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt im Inland"), and
  - holds an unlimited right of residence, or a residence permit under the EU–Switzerland free movement agreement as a Swiss citizen or family member.

3. How this is checked at birth registration (PStV §34). When the birth is registered, the registry office ("das Standesamt") asks whether a parent holds an unlimited right of residence. Where needed, it obtains written information from the Ausländerbehörde. It then examines whether the child acquired German citizenship by birth and records the result.

The excerpts do not set out the procedure for obtaining the child's permit. Whether your child needs an Aufenthaltserlaubnis depends on which of these conditions your family meets. Only the responsible authority decides that. For the residence permit, that is your local Ausländerbehörde. The citizenship check is made by the Standesamt where the birth is registered.

rows.question: We are getting Mutterschaftsgeld. Does that reduce our Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes, as a rule it does. Under the Elterngeld law, Mutterschaftsgeld is "angerechnet" (credited against) Elterngeld.

What the law credits against Elterngeld (BEEG §3(1) no. 1):
- Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) paid under the statutory health insurance rules or the farmers' health insurance rules.
- The employer's top-up to Mutterschaftsgeld under MuSchG §20.

Only amounts due "für die Zeit ab dem Tag der Geburt des Kindes" are credited. These are amounts for the time from the day of birth.

One exception: the Mutterschaftsgeld under MuSchG §19(2) is not credited. That is the payment for women who are not members of a statutory health insurer, at most 210 euros in total, paid by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung.

Part months: if these payments are due for only part of a month of the child's life, they are credited only against the matching part of that month's Elterngeld (BEEG §3(1)).

The 300 euro allowance does not help here. BEEG §3(2) leaves up to 300 euros of Elterngeld free from crediting, but not where income under §3(1) nos. 1 to 3 is credited, and maternity payments fall under no. 1.

The official Familienportal explains the effect for maternity payments for the same child. They are credited in full ("werden komplett auf das Elterngeld angerechnet"). If they are higher than the Elterngeld, only the maternity payments are received. If the Elterngeld is higher, the difference is paid as Elterngeld.

The Familienportal also says two more things. Months in which maternity payments are due for the same child, even for a single day, count as months of the basic form of Elterngeld. And the maternity payments are credited only against the mother's Elterngeld, not against the father's.

How this works out for your family, and any amount you would receive, is decided only by the Elterngeldstelle (Elterngeld office) for your district. That is the office to approach about your own case.

rows.question: Can I work while receiving Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes, the law allows some work while receiving Elterngeld (parental allowance), within limits.

The working-hours condition: one of the conditions for Elterngeld is that you work not at all or not full-time ("keine oder keine volle Erwerbstätigkeit", BEEG §1(1) no. 4). The law says a person is not working full-time if any one of these applies (BEEG §1(6)):
1. their working time does not exceed 32 hours a week on average over the month of the child's life ("32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats");
2. they are in employment for vocational training ("Beschäftigung zur Berufsbildung"); or
3. they work as a suitable childminder within the meaning of §§ 23 and 43 of Book VIII of the Social Code ("Kindertagespflegeperson").

How work affects the amount: the maximum of 1,800 euros a month applies to full months in which you have no income from work (BEEG §2(1)). For months after the birth in which your income from work is lower than before the birth, Elterngeld is paid as the applicable percentage of the difference between the two incomes. For this, income before the birth is counted at most at 2,770 euros (BEEG §2(3)).

Reporting income: if your application states expected income from work during the payment period, the amount is decided provisionally (BEEG §8(3) no. 3). After the payment period ends, you must prove your actual income from work for that time (BEEG §8(1)). If you state that you expect no income from work, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation in case you do have income from work (BEEG §8(2)).

The federal family portal notes that its explanation covers children born after August 2021. For children born before 1 September 2021, partly different rules apply, and it refers parents to their Elterngeldstelle.

Whether you meet these conditions, and how much you would receive while working, is decided by the Elterngeldstelle responsible for you.

rows.question: Where and how do we apply for Kindergeld?
rows.reply:
Where to apply: Kindergeld (child benefit) must be applied for in writing ("schriftlich zu beantragen"), and the application should be filed with the Familienkasse that is responsible under BKGG §13 (BKGG §9(1)). Under BKGG §13(1), the responsible Familienkasse is the one for the district where the claimant has their residence ("Wohnsitz"). If the claimant has no residence in Germany, it is the Familienkasse for the district of their habitual stay. If there is neither, it is the Familienkasse for the district where they work. In all other cases it is the Familienkasse Bayern Nord. The same Familienkasse receives the application and decides on the claim. The official family portal tells applicants to submit the application to the Familienkasse of their Agentur für Arbeit.

How to apply: According to the family portal, you apply either electronically or in writing, using the Familienkassen form. You can fill the form in online, then print and sign it. For newborn children, you can also submit the application entirely online with a valid ELSTER certificate, without printing or signing by hand. The application must include your tax identification number and your child's tax identification number. If the child was born abroad or lives abroad, the Bundesagentur für Arbeit asks for a copy of the foreign birth certificate, or another official document certifying the birth. If the Familienkasse needs more documents, it tells you the date by which to submit them. If you miss that date, your application may be delayed or refused.

Who applies: Kindergeld is paid to only one person per child (BKGG §3(1)). If the child lives in the shared household of both parents, the parents decide between themselves who is the recipient. If they do not decide, the family court decides on application (BKGG §3(2)). Besides the entitled person, anyone with a legitimate interest in the payment may also file the application (BKGG §9(1)).

Applying later: The family portal says Kindergeld can be paid retroactively for up to 6 months ("für bis zu 6 Monate rückwirkend"). If you apply retroactively, state this in the application and say from when you want Kindergeld.

For questions about applying, the portal gives the free service number of the Bundesagentur für Arbeit: 0800 4 555530. Whether Kindergeld is granted in your case is decided by the responsible Familienkasse.

rows.question: What are the Elterngeld rules for a self-employed parent in Bavaria?
rows.reply:
Bavaria is outside the states this product covers. It covers federal law, Hessen state procedures and the Indian consular track. For how Elterngeld (parental allowance) is applied for and handled in Bavaria, go to the Elterngeldstelle responsible for Bavaria, the Zentrum Bayern Familie und Soziales (ZBFS).

The Elterngeld rules themselves are federal law (BEEG), so they apply in Bavaria too. Here is what the excerpts say about self-employed parents.

Which income counts. Elterngeld is 67 percent of income from work before the birth. That income includes positive earnings from "Land- und Forstwirtschaft, Gewerbebetrieb und selbständiger Arbeit" (farming and forestry, trade or business, and self-employed work) that are taxable in Germany. Taxes and social contributions are deducted first, and the result is the monthly average over the assessment period. (BEEG §2(1))

How much at most and at least. The maximum is 1,800 euros a month for full months with no income from work (BEEG §2(1)). The minimum is 300 euros, even with no income from work before the birth (BEEG §2(4)). Where income before the birth was below 1,000 euros, the percentage rises towards 100 percent. Where it was above 1,200 euros, it falls towards 65 percent (BEEG §2(2)).

Working after the birth. If you earn less in a month after the birth than before it, Elterngeld is that percentage of the difference. For this, pre-birth income counts up to 2,770 euros at most (BEEG §2(3)).

How much you may work. One condition of entitlement is that a person does no work or not full-time work (BEEG §1(1)). A person is not working full-time if, among other grounds, their working time does not exceed 32 hours a week on average over the month of the child's life (BEEG §1(6)). People who are self-employed but temporarily not working still count as working ("selbständig erwerbstätig", BEEG §1(6a)).

Provisional decisions. The amount is decided provisionally, based on the information you credibly provide, in each of these cases (BEEG §8(3)):
1. the tax assessment for the last completed tax period before the birth is not yet available, and it cannot yet be said whether the 175,000 euro limit is exceeded;
2. income from work before the birth cannot be determined; or
3. you expect to have income from work during the payment period.

If you stated expected income in the application, you must prove your actual income for that period once the payment period ends (BEEG §8(1)). If you said you would have no income from work, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation in case you do earn (BEEG §8(2)).

Income limit. There is no entitlement if taxable income in the last completed tax period before the birth was more than 175,000 euros. Where two parents both qualify, the limit applies to their combined taxable income (BEEG §1(8)).

The excerpts do not set out how the assessment period is fixed for self-employed income. That is in BEEG §2b, which was not among the excerpts. Whether you qualify and how much you would receive is decided by the Elterngeld authority, not here.

rows.question: Can you fill in our Elterngeld application form for us?
rows.reply:
Filling in your Elterngeld (parental allowance) application is not something this service can do. The form asks for your family's own details and choices, such as which months each parent claims and what income you expect, and those are decisions about your individual case. What the excerpts do say about the application in general is below.

The application must be made in writing. Payment is made retroactively only for the last three months of the child's life before the month in which the application is received, so earlier months are not paid ("rückwirkend nur für die letzten drei Lebensmonate"). The application must state, for each month of the child's life, which type of Elterngeld is being claimed: "Im Antrag ist anzugeben, für welche Lebensmonate Basiselterngeld, für welche Lebensmonate Elterngeld Plus oder für welche Lebensmonate Partnerschaftsbonus beantragt wird." These choices can be changed until the end of the payment period.

The applicant signs the application. The other entitled parent also signs it to confirm they are aware of it. This does not apply where the applicant has sole custody or in the case of § 4c.

According to the federal family portal, the documents to attach are your child's birth certificate and proof of your previous income. For employees, that means payslips for the last 12 months: for mothers, before the month maternity protection begins; for fathers, before the birth. For self-employed people, it is usually the last tax assessment. Further documents may be needed depending on the case.

The responsible authority is the one your Land has designated for the district where your child has their residence in Germany when you first apply. Contact the Elterngeld office for your district. It decides your application.

rows.question: Based on our situation, will our Elterngeld application be approved?
rows.reply:
Whether your application will be approved cannot be answered here. Only the responsible authority decides an individual case: the Elterngeldstelle for your district. What follows is the general rule, not a judgement on your situation.

Conditions the law attaches. Under BEEG §1(1), a person is entitled to Elterngeld (parental allowance) if they:
1. have a residence or habitual abode in Germany,
2. live in one household with their child,
3. look after and raise the child themselves, and
4. are not working, or not working full time.

BEEG §1(6) says a person is not working full time if:
1. their working time does not exceed 32 hours a week on average over the month of the child's life ("32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats"),
2. they are in employment for vocational training, or
3. they work as a suitable childminder within the meaning of §§ 23 and 43 of Book VIII of the Social Code.

BEEG §1(7) adds conditions for foreign nationals who do not have EU freedom of movement. They are entitled only if they:
1. hold a settlement permit or an EU long-term residence permit,
2. hold an EU Blue Card, an ICT card, a mobile ICT card, or a residence permit that entitles or entitled them to work for at least six months. This excludes permits issued for training, au pair or seasonal work, European voluntary service, job search, or recognition of foreign qualifications; permits for study, recognition measures or job search where the person is neither working nor on parental leave under §15 nor receiving ongoing benefits under Book III of the Social Code; and permits under § 23(1) of the Residence Act because of war in the home country, or under § 23a or § 25(3) to (5),
3. hold one of those last-named permits and are lawfully working in Germany, on parental leave under §15, or receiving ongoing benefits under Book III of the Social Code,
4. hold one of those last-named permits and have been in Germany lawfully, with permission or with toleration for at least 15 months, or
5. hold an employment toleration under § 60d with § 60a(2) sentence 3 of the Residence Act.
Minors in this group are entitled regardless of employment under point 3.

Income limit. Under BEEG §1(8), the claim lapses if the taxable income in the last completed assessment period before the birth was more than 175,000 euros ("mehr als 175 000 Euro"). Where another person also meets the household condition, the sum of both persons' taxable income counts.

Applying. Under BEEG §7(1), Elterngeld must be applied for in writing ("schriftlich zu beantragen"). It is paid retroactively only for the last three months of the child's life before the month in which the application is received. Earlier months are not paid.

The Elterngeldstelle for your district is the authority for your application.

rows.question: How much tax will we save if I switch to Steuerklasse 3 before the birth?
rows.reply:
How much tax you would save by switching tax class is a calculation for your own case. This product cannot make it. Tax class choice and its tax effects belong to a tax adviser (Steuerberater) or your local tax office (Finanzamt).

The excerpts do cover how your tax class is used when parental allowance is calculated. This is the general rule, not a verdict on your situation.

- Income before the birth is measured over the twelve calendar months before the month of birth ("die zwölf Kalendermonate vor dem Kalendermonat der Geburt des Kindes").
- The tax deduction in that calculation takes account of the tax class and, where one applies, the factor under § 39f of the Income Tax Act. Tax class VI is disregarded ("die Steuerklasse VI bleibt unberücksichtigt").
- The official family portal explains that the most recent tax class counts. The older tax class is used only if it applied for longer than the newer one within the whole assessment period ("wenn diese innerhalb des gesamten Bemessungszeitraums länger gegolten hat als die neuere").
- According to the same page, a further change of tax class after the birth no longer has any effect on parental allowance.

Whether a switch would change your parental allowance, and by how much, is decided by the parental allowance office (Elterngeldstelle) responsible for your district in Hessen.
